new_points.title: Why is 'vegan' suddenly being used as a slur? | Emma Beddington
new_points.content: US republicans are tarnishing their plant-eating opponents at every opportunity. Yet vegans are perfectly suited to hold power – let me count the waysCool news, fellow soy boys and girls – we’ve been promoted from feeble, tofu-eating wokerati to dangerous radicals unfit for public office. Politico reports that US Republicans have started throwing “vegan” around as a tactic to tarnish their political opponents. “He’s a vegan,” Trump warned of Democratic Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico in May, while Talarico’s opponent, state attorney-general Ken Paxton, is trying to get the nickname “Tofu Talarico” to stick. Paxton also called him “a vegan who thinks God is non-binary”, which I find hilarious as a political put-down – give the man a Netflix special. (Sidenote: I investigated, and according to the Catholic catechism, God is “neither man nor woman”.)Republicans have also been digging up past pro-plant-based statements from Colorado congressional candidate Manny Rutinel: a campaign committee press secretary described him on X as “a far-left vegan activist who wants to end animal agriculture”, posting an old pic of Rutinel bare-chested and wearing a Peta anti-meat banner. Other Dems have also been accused of, erm, liking animals and eating plants: Arizona congressional candidate Amish Shah has been attacked for his “wacky liberal agenda pushing vegan policies” and Lindsay James in Iowa drew heat for merely supporting the idea of “meatless May”. new_points.title: HEPA air purifiers may boost brain function after just one month
new_points.content: Adults aged 40 and older performed about 12% faster on a test of executive function after using a HEPA air purifier at home for one month. The findings suggest that cleaner indoor air could offer a simple way to help protect the brain from the effects of traffic-related pollution.

new_points.title: Hundreds of hidden earthquakes found at Antarctica’s Doomsday Glacier
new_points.content: Hundreds of previously overlooked seismic events have been detected beneath Antarctica, including 245 near the marine edge of the Thwaites Glacier. Many appear to be glacial earthquakes caused when huge icebergs break off, capsize, and collide with the glacier. The surge in activity coincided with a period when Thwaites was flowing faster toward the ocean, hinting that changing ocean conditions may be destabilizing the ice.

new_points.title: Researchers unveil sustainable spirulina solution to vitamin B12 deficiency
new_points.content: Researchers have produced a form of Spirulina containing biologically active vitamin B12 at levels comparable to beef. By carefully controlling the light used to grow the algae, they overcame a major problem with conventional Spirulina, which mainly contains a form of B12 the human body cannot use. The carbon-neutral system could provide a more sustainable source of the essential vitamin.

new_points.title: This strange “spacetime crystal” can suddenly become a black hole
new_points.content: Physicists have mathematically captured a bizarre “spacetime crystal” that can either dissolve or collapse into a microscopic black hole after only a tiny change in energy. Their breakthrough came from an unusual trick involving infinitely many dimensions, potentially giving researchers a new tool for studying primordial and microscopic black holes.

new_points.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
new_points.content: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

new_points.title: The next Cascadia megaquake could hit Oregon harder than expected
new_points.content: The Juan de Fuca plate beneath northern Oregon appears to be shallower than previously estimated, potentially making shaking from a future Cascadia megathrust earthquake significantly stronger. Scientists also found a deep basin beneath Tillamook that could trap seismic waves and intensify the shaking even further.

new_points.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
new_points.content: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

new_points.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
new_points.content: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

new_points.title: Scientists discover a massive heat anomaly deep inside Mars
new_points.content: Mars has a hidden temperature divide, with its southern interior potentially hundreds of degrees hotter than the north and partially molten. The discovery could help explain several long-standing Martian mysteries, including unusual magnetism, seismic behavior, and clues to the planet’s ancient water history.

new_points.title: A cancer therapy put severe rheumatoid arthritis into remission
new_points.content: CAR T-cell therapy dramatically reduced disease activity in six people with severe rheumatoid arthritis that had resisted other treatments, with three achieving medication-free remission. The treatment may work by clearing out harmful immune cells and effectively rebooting part of the immune system, although much larger studies are still needed.

new_points.title: Some signs of quantum gravity may be an illusion
new_points.content: Quantum mechanics and Einstein’s theory of gravity explain almost everything we see in nature, yet physicists still do not know how to unite them. A new theoretical framework suggests that some experiments that appear to show gravity behaving quantum mechanically may have a much more ordinary explanation. Researchers found that scenarios involving a supposed “superposition of gravity” can sometimes be described equally well as quantum particles moving through classical spacetime.

new_points.title: A new recipe unlocks “impossible” nanocrystals for LEDs, implants, and superconductors
new_points.content: Scientists have cracked a long-standing chemistry problem, creating nanocrystals from tough metal nitrides that were previously extremely difficult to produce at this scale. The breakthrough could turn familiar materials used in LEDs, implants, and superconductors into building blocks for flexible electronics, printable devices, and other technologies.

new_points.content: Pointed offers a strategic twist to the news quiz format, testing not just players’ knowledge of the news but also their confidence in their answers. new_points.title: Rep. Krishnamoorthi Warns Iran War Weakens US in Asia
new_points.content: Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi (D) says the Iran war is depleting key US munitions and pulling military assets from the Indo Pacific, potentially weakening deterrence against China as concerns over Taiwan grow. While on Bloomberg This Weekend, the Illinois Democrat also criticized the administration’s trade fight with Canada and Venezuela oil policy while calling for more US assistance to Nepal following catastrophic flooding. (Source: Bloomberg)

new_points.title: How YouTube Filmmakers Are Reshaping Hollywood’s Talent Pipeline
new_points.content: YouTube creators are turning online audiences into big-screen opportunities, with filmmakers like Alex Kister moving from DIY horror videos to studio deals. As platforms, distributors and FAST services open new paths to money and viewers, the creator boom is also flooding the market with content, making it easier to start but harder to win. (Source: Bloomberg)

new_points.title: Investors Bet on a Hair Loss Treatment Boom
new_points.content: Drugmakers are developing a new generation of hair loss treatments, including lotions, pills and longer-lasting injections, targeting a US market where tens of millions of men and women experience pattern hair loss. Joining Christina Ruffini and Bailey Lipschultz on Bloomberg This Weekend is Bloomberg News Equities Reporter Avalon Pernell says some treatments could seek approval and reach the market as soon as 2027, drawing investor interest in companies hoping to tap consumers already willing to spend heavily on hair restoration. (Source: Bloomberg)

new_points.title: Shein’s $100 Billion Valuation Falls to $26 Billion
new_points.content: Shein is heading toward a Hong Kong listing at a valuation of about $26.5 billion, roughly a quarter of its 2022 peak, after earlier efforts to list in New York and London ran into regulatory hurdles. Bloomberg News Consumer Finance Reporter Lisa Du is on Bloomberg This Weekend with hosts Christina Ruffini and Bailey Lipschultz and says the fast-fashion giant is pitching investors on expanding beyond its core brand by acquiring or partnering with other labels, even as geopolitical, regulatory and reputational risks weigh on its growth story. (Source: Bloomberg)

new_points.title: Venezuela Oil Deal Raises Questions Over US Role
new_points.content: The Trump administration’s deal giving a US-led venture access to 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil could reshape the countries’ economic relationship, but questions remain over its political durability and whether it will provoke a backlash inside Venezuela. Former Deputy National Secuirty Advisor for Middle East Affairs and the Heritage Foundation's Victoria Coates is on Bloomberg This Weekend and argues the agreement could encourage US investment and restore Venezuela’s energy sector, but says economic development must ultimately be accompanied by political liberalization and self-determination. (Source: Bloomberg)

new_points.title: Gold Bulls Turn to Exotic Options, Spreads in ‘Orderly’ Rally

new_points.title: Iceland Rejects Restarting EU Membership Talks
new_points.content: Icelandic voters rejected restarting EU accession talks, with opposition particularly strong outside Reykjavik as concerns over sovereignty, fisheries and agriculture outweighed arguments for closer European ties. RÚV Iceland News Defense & Security Correspondent Ingólfur Sigfússon is on Bloomberg This Weekend and says says the result puts membership talks on hold and could shift attention toward Norway as Nordic countries reassess their relationships with Europe amid geopolitical uncertainty. (Source: Bloomberg)

new_points.title: Dollar Debasement Backs Bull Case for Emerging Bonds, Funds Say

new_points.title: NASA’s Roman Telescope Takes Aim at Cosmic Mysteries
new_points.content: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy on a mission to study dark energy, dark matter and planets beyond our solar system. Roman is headed about 1 million miles from Earth to Lagrange point 2, where its wide field of view will allow scientists to survey billions of galaxies far faster than the Hubble telescope. Joining Bloomberg This Weekend to watch the launch with hosts Christina Ruffini and Bailey Lipschultz is Space Network Co-Founder and COO Ross Hamilton to discuss the telescope's mission. (Source: Bloomberg)
